FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: sorghum tô
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a {0_adj} paste beaten with a spatula until it turns smooth and firm, served with a stringing {1_adj} sauce. You take a ball of it in your right hand, hollow it with your thumb, and dip.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: tuwo dawa
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: the Hausa version: a {0_adj} ball moulded with a ladle, with a miyan kuka of pounded baobab leaves and a {2_adj} sauce. Baobab thickens without any flour at all.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: fura da nono
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: balls of cooked {0_adj}, pounded with {2_plur} and ginger, crushed into the fermented {1_coll} of the Fulani herders. Drunk from a calabash, it stands in for a whole meal on the road.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: sorghum ogi
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {0_coll} soaked three days, ground, sieved and left to sour, then cooked into a smooth gruel. Sour, {1_adj} and scented with {2_plur}: the breakfast of half of West Africa.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: kisra
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a fermented {0_adj} batter spread into a veil over a scorching plate, so fine that it cooks in ten seconds. Stacked by the dozen, it serves as the plate for a {1_adj} and {2_adj} mullah.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: sorghum asida
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a {0_adj} paste worked to elasticity, hollowed into a well at the centre and filled with melted {1_coll} and {2_coll}. Eaten from the edges towards the middle, by several people out of one dish.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: sorghum injera
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a {0_adj} batter fermented three days, poured in a spiral over the plate and covered: the bubbles that break the surface make the eyes. Loaded with a {1_adj} and {2_adj} misir wat.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: sorghum genfo

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: ting ya mabele
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {0_coll} left to ferment several days before it is cooked, which gives it its frank sourness, served with {2_coll} and curdled {1_coll}. The national dish of Botswana, eaten morning and evening.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: jowar khichdi
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {0_coll} cracked and {1_coll} cooked together until they can no longer be told apart, lifted by a tempering of {2_adj} toasted in ghee. The dish served to convalescents.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.label: jowar dosa
FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a batter of {0_adj}, {1_adj} and {2_adj} fermented overnight, spread in a spiral over the plate and cooked until the edges crisp.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a thick flatbread of several flours mixed together, loaded with raw {1_adj} and {2_adj}, flattened straight into the pan with wetted fingers and pierced with a hole at the centre.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {1_coll} cooked with a handful of {0_adj} and {2_adj}, which stain it a dark red. It was served to children on their first birthday, to keep ill fortune away.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: small cakes of sticky {0_adj} fried in the pan and then folded into half-moons over a sweetened {1_adj} paste. The sorghum gives them a rust colour and a taste of hazelnut.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: whole {0_coll} boiled an hour until it splits without falling apart, mixed with roasted {1_plur} and toasted {2_plur}. It stays firm under the tooth, unlike every other grain.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {0_coll} thrown by the handful into a scorching pan: the grains burst into minute white balls, ten times smaller than popcorn, and a great deal more tender.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {2_adj} scones split open scalding and drowned in sorghum {1_plur}, dark and bitter under the sweetness. The syrup and the grain come from the same plant, pressed or threshed.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: a dough of sorghum {1_adj} and ground {2_adj}, baked briefly so as to stay soft in the middle and crazed on top.

FlavorText.FlavorDef.description: {1_coll} drowned in a {2_adj} filling bound with {0_adj} syrup, less cloying than corn syrup and a great deal deeper. The pie of Kentucky and Tennessee.
